issue.title: fix(cli): deploy hangs forever when an AWS call gets no response
issue.body:
A deploy that got no answer from AWS used to wait until the job was killed, and now each silent call is dropped after 5 minutes and retried.

**What this code is for**

`sdkRequestHandler` in `packages/@aws-cdk/toolkit-lib/lib/api/aws-auth/awscli-compatible.ts` builds the HTTP settings that every AWS SDK client in the CLI and in the toolkit library uses. Both `packages/aws-cdk/lib/cli/cli.ts` (with the proxy agent, if any) and `Toolkit.sdkProvider` in `toolkit.ts` (with `sdkConfig.httpOptions.agent`, if any) call it, and the result is passed to every client next to a `ConfiguredRetryStrategy` that retries timeouts and other network errors. The one exception after this PR is `invokeCommand` in `SDK.lambda()` in `sdk.ts`, which uses a longer idle timeout.

**Before this PR**

A GitHub Actions job runs `cdk deploy`, and the connection under one `DescribeStacks` call goes silent after the request was sent, as described in #2097.

1. The CloudFormation client sends `DescribeStacks` through `NodeHttpHandler` with `connectionTimeout: 10000` and `requestTimeout: 300000`.
2. The connection was already open, so `connectionTimeout` never applies.
3. After 300000 ms the `requestTimeout` passes. `throwOnRequestTimeout` is not set, so Smithy only logs `[WARN] a request has exceeded the configured 300000 ms requestTimeout`.
4. The request is never failed, so `ConfiguredRetryStrategy` never sees an error and never retries.
5. The CLI waits on that same request with no further output. In the report on #2097 that was almost 6 hours, until the GitHub job timeout cancelled it. Against a local server that accepts and never replies, I saw the same thing on `main`: one connection, the warning at 300 s, and still waiting at 330 s.

**After this PR**

Same job, same silent `DescribeStacks` call.

1. Same as above, but the settings now also carry `socketTimeout: 300000`.
2. Once no data has moved in either direction for 300 seconds, Smithy destroys the request and rejects it with a `TimeoutError`.
3. `ConfiguredRetryStrategy` treats `TimeoutError` as a temporary error and sends the call again on a new connection.
4. If the new connection answers, the deploy carries on. If every attempt stays silent, the command fails with that `TimeoutError` instead of waiting. There are 7 attempts in total, so that is about 35 minutes plus the short retry delays. Against the same silent local server with a 60 s value, I saw the call retried on connections 2 to 7 and then failed at about 467 s, which is the same path with a shorter timer.
5. A slow call that keeps sending or receiving data, such as a large asset upload, never goes 300 seconds without data, so it is not cut off.
6. A hotswap of a `BucketDeployment` invokes its Lambda function synchronously, and Lambda sends nothing back until the function returns, which can take up to 15 minutes. `Invoke` therefore gets `socketTimeout: 960000`, which covers that maximum plus cold start init, so a long `s3 sync` is never dropped and started again while it is still running.

**The diagram**

```mermaid
flowchart LR

classDef box fill:#eef1ff,stroke:#4c5bd4,color:#111827
classDef bad fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#cc0000,color:#111827,stroke-width:3px
classDef good fill:#c8f0c8,stroke:#008800,color:#111827,stroke-width:3px

subgraph BEFORE["BEFORE: waits until the job is killed, 1 connection"]
direction TB
  B1["cdk deploy calls DescribeStacks"] --> B2["NodeHttpHandler sends the request"]
  B2 --> B3["connection goes silent"]
  B3 --> B4{"requestTimeout 300000 passes"}
  B4 -->|"throwOnRequestTimeout not set"| B5["logs WARN and keeps waiting forever"]
  B4 -->|"response arrives"| B6["deploy continues"]
end

subgraph AFTER["AFTER: retried every 300 s, then fails with TimeoutError"]
direction TB
  A1["cdk deploy calls DescribeStacks"] --> A2["NodeHttpHandler sends the request"]
  A2 --> A3["connection goes silent"]
  A3 --> A4{"THE CHANGE: socketTimeout 300000"}
  A4 -->|"no data for 300 s"| A5["TimeoutError, retried on a new connection"]
  A4 -->|"data still moving"| A6["slow upload keeps going"]
end

B1 ~~~ A1

class B1,B2,B3,B6 box
class A1,A2,A3,A6 box
class B4,B5 bad
class A4,A5 good

linkStyle 3 stroke:#cc0000,stroke-width:5px
linkStyle 8 stroke:#008800,stroke-width:5px

style BEFORE fill:#fff5f5,stroke:#cc0000,color:#111827
style AFTER fill:#f3fff3,stroke:#008800,color:#111827
```

**The change**

- `sdkRequestHandler` now returns `socketTimeout: 300000` next to the existing `connectionTimeout` and `requestTimeout`. This is the fix. I reused the 300 seconds that `requestTimeout` already has, because the Smithy docs for `throwOnRequestTimeout` say `requestTimeout` "was for a long time incorrectly being set as a socket idle timeout". So the CLI already ran with a 5 minute idle timeout that threw for years, and this brings that behavior back on purpose.
- `SDK.lambda()` in `sdk.ts` sends `Invoke` through a second client, created on the first invoke, with `socketTimeout: 960000` and every other setting unchanged. If the caller already set `socketTimeout` to 0 (no timeout) or to something longer, `Invoke` keeps that value. The other Lambda calls, such as `UpdateFunctionCode` and the hotswap waiters, keep the shared 300 s value, so a silent one of those is not held for 16 minutes per attempt. The hotswap of a `BucketDeployment` calls `Invoke` synchronously and the function may run for the full 15 minutes, so a shorter idle timeout would drop it and the retries would start overlapping `s3 sync --delete` runs.
- `RequestHandlerSettings` in `base-credentials.ts` gets an optional `socketTimeout` field, so the value type checks and a custom `IBaseCredentialsProvider` receives it in `clientConfig.requestHandler` too.
- `requestTimeout` and its warning are left as they are. I did not turn on `throwOnRequestTimeout`, because that timer runs from the start of the request until the response headers arrive, so it would fail a healthy upload that takes longer than 5 minutes. @JimNero009 pointed this out in the issue, and their suggestion of a `socketTimeout` is what this PR follows. Thank you for the very clear report and reproduction.
- Tests in `awscli-compatible.test.ts`: one checks the settings `sdkRequestHandler` returns, including the agent on both `httpAgent` and `httpsAgent`, and fails without this change. Two more run a real `STSClient` against a local TCP server with a 1 s `socketTimeout`. To be honest about what these two prove: they pass on `main` too, because they check how Smithy handles `socketTimeout` rather than this change. I kept them as a guard in case a future Smithy version changes that behavior, but I am very happy to drop them if you would rather not have a TCP server in a unit suite: a server that never answers gets a second connection and the call rejects with `TimeoutError`; a server that sends its whole response, headers included, in small pieces every 50 ms still succeeds on one connection. That second test fails if the settings use `requestTimeout` with `throwOnRequestTimeout` instead, which is why I went with `socketTimeout`.
- Tests in `sdk.test.ts`: one checks that `invokeCommand` is sent through a client with `socketTimeout: 960000` and the other settings unchanged, and fails without this change; four check that a disabled or longer caller value is kept and a shorter or unset one is raised to 960000; one checks the `Invoke` client is created only on the first invoke; two check that other Lambda calls and the CloudFormation client still get the shared settings.

I would really value your view on a few choices, and I am happy to change any of them:

- 300 seconds restores the old behavior. Would you prefer something shorter, such as the 60 to 120 seconds the issue suggested? If so, I would be glad to check the other clients for calls that can stay silent that long, the way the Lambda one does.
- The issue also asks for these timeouts to be configurable. I left that out to keep this small, but I can add it here or in a follow up if you think it belongs.
- The standalone `cdk-assets` CLI builds its clients in `cdk-assets-lib/lib/aws.ts` without any of these timeouts. Would you like the same change there as a separate PR?

**What changes for a user**

- A deploy, bootstrap or any other command whose AWS call goes silent no longer hangs. Each silent attempt is dropped after 5 minutes and retried.
- If AWS never answers at all, the command now fails with a `TimeoutError` after the existing retries, about 35 minutes, instead of running until the CI job is killed.
- Calls that answer normally, and slow calls that keep moving data such as large asset uploads, behave exactly as before.
- `cdk deploy --hotswap` and `cdk watch` with a `BucketDeployment` that takes many minutes keep working, because `Invoke` waits up to 16 minutes.
- A call that changes state, such as `ExecuteChangeSet` or `Invoke`, is now retried after a silent timeout instead of hanging. If AWS did process the first attempt, the retry can fail with a clearer error such as an existing change set. This is the same tradeoff the SDK already makes for a reset connection.
- Proxy users are covered, because the proxy agent goes through the same `sdkRequestHandler`.
- The `requestTimeout` warning after 5 minutes still appears for very long uploads, as it does today.

Fixes #2097

### Checklist

- [ ] This change contains a major version upgrade for a dependency and I confirm all breaking changes are addressed
  - Release notes for the new version:

In 0f50cb8a and c8300d56 I raised the Lambda `Invoke` idle timeout from 905 s to 960 s to leave room for cold start init, moved that longer timeout onto `Invoke` only so other Lambda calls like the hotswap waiters keep the shared 300 s, and widened the margin in the slow response test so it should not flake on a busy runner. The PR description is updated to match. Does scoping it to `Invoke` like that seem right to you?

issue.title: fix(s3): notifications cleanup fails when bucket is already deleted

labels.name: repo-67fb60d4

issue.body:
### Issue # (if applicable)

Closes #35352.

Deleting a stack whose bucket has event notifications could get stuck forever once the bucket was gone; now the cleanup step sees the bucket is gone and lets the deletion finish.

**What this code is for**

`bucket.addEventNotification()` adds a `Custom::S3BucketNotifications` resource backed by a small Python Lambda, `index.py` in `notifications-resource-handler`. CloudFormation calls its `handler()` on Create, Update and Delete. On Delete it writes an empty (or, for an imported bucket, an external only) configuration with `put_bucket_notification_configuration`, and for an imported bucket it first reads the current one with `get_bucket_notification_configuration`.

**Before this PR**

A developer runs `cdk destroy` on a stack with a bucket and `bucket.addEventNotification(...)`.

1. The bucket is already gone when the Delete runs, for example after an earlier failed delete attempt (as @rittneje describes) or after it was removed outside the stack.
2. CloudFormation sends a `Delete` request to `handler()`.
3. `handler()` calls `put_bucket_notification_configuration` (or `get_bucket_notification_configuration` first, for an imported bucket).
4. S3 answers with a `ClientError` whose code is `NoSuchBucket`.
5. The `except Exception` block reports `FAILED` for every error, including this one.
6. The stack goes to `DELETE_FAILED`, and every retry repeats steps 2 to 5, so the stack can never be deleted.

**After this PR**

Same developer, same `cdk destroy`. Same as above through step 4.

5. The `except` block now checks: is this a `Delete` request, and is the error a `ClientError` with code `NoSuchBucket`?
6. Yes, so it prints `Bucket no longer exists, nothing to clean up` and reports `SUCCESS`.
7. The stack finishes deleting.
8. If the error is anything else, for example `AccessDenied`, or if `NoSuchBucket` comes back on a `Create` or `Update`, the handler reports `FAILED` exactly as before.

**The diagram**

```mermaid
flowchart LR

classDef box fill:#eef1ff,stroke:#4c5bd4,color:#111827
classDef bad fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#cc0000,color:#111827,stroke-width:3px
classDef good fill:#c8f0c8,stroke:#008800,color:#111827,stroke-width:3px

subgraph BEFORE["BEFORE: every delete and every retry fails"]
direction TB
  B1["cdk destroy, bucket already gone"] --> B2["handler() gets RequestType Delete"]
  B2 --> B3["S3 returns ClientError NoSuchBucket"]
  B3 --> B4{"except Exception: any error?"}
  B4 -->|"NoSuchBucket counts as an error"| B5["FAILED, stack stuck in DELETE_FAILED"]
  B4 -->|"no error"| B6["SUCCESS"]
end

subgraph AFTER["AFTER: the delete finishes in one try"]
direction TB
  A1["cdk destroy, bucket already gone"] --> A2["handler() gets RequestType Delete"]
  A2 --> A3["S3 returns ClientError NoSuchBucket"]
  A3 --> A4{"THE CHANGE: Delete and code is NoSuchBucket?"}
  A4 -->|"yes, nothing left to clean"| A5["SUCCESS, stack deletes"]
  A4 -->|"no, e.g. AccessDenied"| A6["FAILED, same as before"]
end

B1 ~~~ A1

class B1,B2,B3,B6 box
class A1,A2,A3,A6 box
class B4,B5 bad
class A4,A5 good

linkStyle 3 stroke:#cc0000,stroke-width:5px
linkStyle 8 stroke:#008800,stroke-width:5px

style BEFORE fill:#fff5f5,stroke:#cc0000,color:#111827
style AFTER fill:#f3fff3,stroke:#008800,color:#111827
```

**The change**

The fix is in the `except` block of `handler()`:

```python
if event.get("RequestType") == "Delete" and is_missing_bucket(e):
  print("Bucket no longer exists, nothing to clean up")
else:
  # unchanged: log, FAILED, error message
```

`is_missing_bucket` checks the structured error, `isinstance(error, ClientError)` and `error.response["Error"]["Code"] == "NoSuchBucket"`, not the message text. Because the check sits in `handler()`, it covers both managed buckets and imported buckets (`Managed: false`), whether the error comes from the read or the write. All destination types (SNS, SQS and Lambda) go through this one handler, so all of them are covered.

**What changes for a user**

- `cdk destroy` on a stack with bucket notifications now completes when the bucket is already gone, for SNS, SQS and Lambda destinations alike.
- A stack that is already stuck in `DELETE_FAILED` cannot receive the new handler through an update, so it still needs `aws cloudformation delete-stack --retain-resources` for the notifications resource, or the `FORCE_DELETE_STACK` deletion mode.
- Real errors still fail the delete: `AccessDenied`, throttling, anything that is not `NoSuchBucket`.
- `NoSuchBucket` on `Create` or `Update` still fails, because there it means a real problem.
- Create and Update behaviour is otherwise unchanged.

---

### Reason for this change

Thank you @aramfe for the clear report, and @pahud for confirming it and for describing the fix: let the Delete in `NotificationsResourceHandler` succeed on `NoSuchBucket`. @rittneje's point shaped this PR too: fixing the order between the two resources would not be enough, since CloudFormation still deletes the bucket when the custom resource fails, and the retry then fails forever. So the handler has to accept that the bucket is gone.

I also read the two earlier attempts, #35388 and #35481, which went in the same direction. In this PR:

- The handler change is 2 files.
- The decision uses the `ClientError` code only, and only on Delete, so every other failure is still reported.

On #35481, @TheRealAmazonKendra suggested fixing the dependency between the bucket and the notifications resource instead, and asked which destination types are affected. That resource already depends on the bucket, so CloudFormation normally deletes it first; the trouble starts when the bucket is gone anyway, and @rittneje's comment explains why ordering alone cannot help then. Every destination type (SNS, SQS, Lambda) shares this one handler, so they are all affected and all covered here. I would really value your view on whether this handler change is enough on its own, or whether you would like a dependency change as well.

### Description of changes

See "The change" above. One new helper, `is_missing_bucket`, and one `if` in the `except` block of `handler()`. No change to the TypeScript constructs.

### Describe any new or updated permissions being added

None.

### Description of how you validated changes

- New `MissingBucketTest` in `test_index.py`. It covers managed and imported buckets, `NoSuchBucket` raised from the read or the write, `AccessDenied` on Delete, and `NoSuchBucket` on Create and Update. The three Delete cases fail on `main` and pass with this change. All 25 handler tests pass on Python 3.9 and 3.13.
- I could not deploy the integration tests myself, so I did not run them against an AWS account. Could a maintainer add `pr/needs-integration-tests-deployment` when you have a moment?
- This PR has no new integ test file, because a bucket that is missing during Delete cannot be set up in an integ test, and the existing integ tests already deploy this handler. If that sounds reasonable to you, could a maintainer also add `pr-linter/exempt-integ-test`? I am glad to add a test instead if you see a way to set it up.

### Checklist

- [x] My code adheres to the [CONTRIBUTING GUIDE](https://github.com/aws/aws-cdk/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [DESIGN GUIDELINES](https://github.com/aws/aws-cdk/blob/main/docs/DESIGN_GUIDELINES.md)

---

If you see a way to cover it in an integ test that I missed, I'd be glad to add it. Would you like anything changed?

issue.title: fix(lambda): `LambdaTarget` fails with `skipPermissions` functions

labels.name: repo-67fb60d4
labels.description: This issue is a bug.

labels.name: user-3784fdbb/repo-7839c985
labels.description: Medium work item – several days of effort

labels.name: repo-67fb60d4

labels.name: user-6302958c/repo-eb7dcc0a

issue.body:
### Issue # (if applicable)

Closes #35559.

Putting a Lambda function from another account or environment behind a load balancer crashed `cdk synth` even when you said its permissions are handled elsewhere; now synth succeeds.

**What this code is for**

`LambdaTarget` puts a Lambda function behind an application or network load balancer target group. When the target group is created, it calls `fn.grantInvoke(new iam.ServicePrincipal('elasticloadbalancing.amazonaws.com'))` so the load balancer may call the function, then `grant.applyBefore(targetGroup)` so CloudFormation creates that permission before the target group. `grantInvoke` ends up in the private `grant()` method of `FunctionBase`, which hands `iam.Grant` a stand in resource whose `addToResourcePolicy` creates the `AWS::Lambda::Permission`.

**Before this PR**

A developer imports a function with `Function.fromFunctionAttributes(stack, 'Fn', { functionArn, skipPermissions: true })` in an environment agnostic stack, as in the issue, and adds `new LambdaTarget(fn)` to an `ApplicationTargetGroup`.

1. The target group calls `attachToApplicationTargetGroup`, which calls `fn.grantInvoke(...)`.
2. `grant()` calls `addPermission`. The function cannot have its permissions changed, so `addPermission` returns without creating a `CfnPermission`.
3. `grant()` sees `skipPermissions` is set, so it does not throw, and returns `{ statementAdded: true, policyDependable: undefined }`.
4. `Grant` reads `statementAdded: true` with no dependable and falls back to `options.resource`, which is the stand in object from `grant()`.
5. `grant.applyBefore(targetGroup)` adds the grant as a dependency of the target group.
6. At synth, the grant asks the stand in object for its dependency roots and fails: `[object Object] does not implement IDependable`. The same thing happens with `NetworkTargetGroup`.

**After this PR**

Same developer, same code. Same as above through step 2.

3. `grant()` returns `{ statementAdded: false, policyDependable: undefined }`, because no permission was created.
4. `Grant` keeps the policy statement, so `grant.success` is still `true`, and it has nothing to depend on.
5. `grant.applyBefore(targetGroup)` adds no dependency.
6. Synth succeeds. The target group points at the function ARN and there is no `AWS::Lambda::Permission`, which is what `skipPermissions` asks for.

When the permission can be created (a function in the same stack, or an imported function or alias in the same account), `addPermission` creates the `CfnPermission`, `statementAdded` is `true`, and the target group still has `DependsOn` on it, exactly as today.

**The diagram**

```mermaid
flowchart LR

classDef box fill:#eef1ff,stroke:#4c5bd4,color:#111827
classDef bad fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#cc0000,color:#111827,stroke-width:3px
classDef good fill:#c8f0c8,stroke:#008800,color:#111827,stroke-width:3px

subgraph BEFORE["BEFORE: cdk synth fails"]
direction TB
  B1["LambdaTarget on an imported function"] --> B2["fn.grantInvoke calls grant()"]
  B2 --> B3["skipPermissions: no CfnPermission created"]
  B3 --> B4{"statementAdded: true"}
  B4 -->|"no permission, stand in object kept"| B5["synth fails: does not implement IDependable"]
  B4 -->|"permission created"| B6["TargetGroup DependsOn the permission"]
end

subgraph AFTER["AFTER: cdk synth succeeds"]
direction TB
  A1["LambdaTarget on an imported function"] --> A2["fn.grantInvoke calls grant()"]
  A2 --> A3["skipPermissions: no CfnPermission created"]
  A3 --> A4{"THE CHANGE: statementAdded = permissionNode !== undefined"}
  A4 -->|"no permission"| A5["nothing to depend on, synth succeeds"]
  A4 -->|"permission created"| A6["TargetGroup DependsOn the permission, as before"]
end

B1 ~~~ A1

class B1,B2,B3,B6 box
class A1,A2,A3,A6 box
class B4,B5 bad
class A4,A5 good

linkStyle 3 stroke:#cc0000,stroke-width:5px
linkStyle 8 stroke:#008800,stroke-width:5px

style BEFORE fill:#fff5f5,stroke:#cc0000,color:#111827
style AFTER fill:#f3fff3,stroke:#008800,color:#111827
```

**The change**

One line in `packages/aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda/lib/function-base.ts`, inside the `addToResourcePolicy` of the private `grant()`:

```ts
return { statementAdded: permissionNode !== undefined, policyDependable: permissionNode };
```

`AddToResourcePolicyResult` documents that when `statementAdded` is `true` and no `policyDependable` is given, the resource object itself is used as the dependable. The stand in object in `grant()` is not dependable, so `statementAdded` now says `true` only when a `CfnPermission` really exists. The `ValidationError` for functions without `skipPermissions` is untouched.

Thank you @alex-at-cascade for the clear report and both repros, and @pahud for confirming it and pointing at the `grantInvoke` then `applyBefore` path. I first tried the check inside `LambdaTarget` that @pahud suggested, but `Grant` does not expose `policyDependable` publicly, so I followed @alex-at-cascade's idea that the grant itself should know, and fixed it where the grant result is built. That also covers anyone else who calls `applyBefore` on such a grant, for example `RotationSchedule` in `aws-secretsmanager` with a rotation function imported using `skipPermissions`. If you would rather keep this change inside `aws-elasticloadbalancingv2-targets`, I am very happy to move it.

Tests: in `lambda-target.test.ts`, for both `ApplicationTargetGroup` and `NetworkTargetGroup`, a function in the same stack, an imported alias in the same account, and an imported function with `skipPermissions`; in `function.test.ts`, `applyBefore` on a `skipPermissions` grant. The two `skipPermissions` target group tests and the `function.test.ts` test fail on `main` with the `IDependable` error and pass with this change.

**What changes for a user**

- `LambdaTarget` with a function imported using `skipPermissions` now synthesizes for both application and network target groups, with no `AWS::Lambda::Permission` and no `DependsOn`.
- Functions in the same stack and imported functions or aliases whose permissions can be created behave exactly as before, same permission, same `DependsOn`.
- Any other `grantInvoke(...).applyBefore(...)` on a `skipPermissions` function no longer crashes synth.
- An imported alias from `Alias.fromAliasAttributes` in a stack where its permissions cannot be changed still throws the existing `Cannot modify permission to lambda function` error, which points to `fromFunctionAttributes` with `skipPermissions`, and that path now works. I left this alone on purpose and would really value your view. Would you prefer `LambdaTarget` to warn with `Annotations` and skip the permission, the way `LambdaIntegration` does through `addPermission`, or a `skipPermissions` option on `AliasAttributes`, or keeping the error as it is? I am glad to follow up with whichever you think fits best.

### Reason for this change

`LambdaTarget` crashed synth for functions imported with `skipPermissions`, described above.

### Description of changes

See "The change" above.

### Describe any new or updated permissions being added

None. When `skipPermissions` is set, no permission was created before and none is created now.

### Description of how you validated changes

Unit tests described above, plus the existing `aws-lambda`, `aws-elasticloadbalancingv2`, `aws-elasticloadbalancingv2-targets`, `aws-secretsmanager`, `aws-apigateway`, `aws-events-targets` and `aws-iam` suites. No snapshot changes, since templates that synthesized before are unchanged.

### Checklist
- [x] My code adheres to the [CONTRIBUTING GUIDE](https://github.com/aws/aws-cdk/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [DESIGN GUIDELINES](https://github.com/aws/aws-cdk/blob/main/docs/DESIGN_GUIDELINES.md)

----

If you'd rather have an integ test after all, I'm glad to add one, or to change anything else about the fix. Is there anything that would make this easier to review?

issue.title: fix(cli): deploy hangs forever when an AWS call gets no response
issue.body:
A deploy that got no answer from AWS used to wait until the job was killed, and now each silent call is dropped after 5 minutes and retried.

**What this code is for**

`sdkRequestHandler` in `packages/@aws-cdk/toolkit-lib/lib/api/aws-auth/awscli-compatible.ts` builds the HTTP settings that every AWS SDK client in the CLI and in the toolkit library uses. Both `packages/aws-cdk/lib/cli/cli.ts` (with the proxy agent, if any) and `Toolkit.sdkProvider` in `toolkit.ts` (with `sdkConfig.httpOptions.agent`, if any) call it, and the result is passed to every client next to a `ConfiguredRetryStrategy` that retries timeouts and other network errors. The one exception after this PR is `invokeCommand` in `SDK.lambda()` in `sdk.ts`, which uses a longer idle timeout.

**Before this PR**

A GitHub Actions job runs `cdk deploy`, and the connection under one `DescribeStacks` call goes silent after the request was sent, as described in #2097.

1. The CloudFormation client sends `DescribeStacks` through `NodeHttpHandler` with `connectionTimeout: 10000` and `requestTimeout: 300000`.
2. The connection was already open, so `connectionTimeout` never applies.
3. After 300000 ms the `requestTimeout` passes. `throwOnRequestTimeout` is not set, so Smithy only logs `[WARN] a request has exceeded the configured 300000 ms requestTimeout`.
4. The request is never failed, so `ConfiguredRetryStrategy` never sees an error and never retries.
5. The CLI waits on that same request with no further output. In the report on #2097 that was almost 6 hours, until the GitHub job timeout cancelled it. Against a local server that accepts and never replies, I saw the same thing on `main`: one connection, the warning at 300 s, and still waiting at 330 s.

**After this PR**

Same job, same silent `DescribeStacks` call.

1. Same as above, but the settings now also carry `socketTimeout: 300000`.
2. Once no data has moved in either direction for 300 seconds, Smithy destroys the request and rejects it with a `TimeoutError`.
3. `ConfiguredRetryStrategy` treats `TimeoutError` as a temporary error and sends the call again on a new connection.
4. If the new connection answers, the deploy carries on. If every attempt stays silent, the command fails with that `TimeoutError` instead of waiting. There are 7 attempts in total, so that is about 35 minutes plus the short retry delays. Against the same silent local server with a 60 s value, I saw the call retried on connections 2 to 7 and then failed at about 467 s, which is the same path with a shorter timer.
5. A slow call that keeps sending or receiving data, such as a large asset upload, never goes 300 seconds without data, so it is not cut off.
6. A hotswap of a `BucketDeployment` invokes its Lambda function synchronously, and Lambda sends nothing back until the function returns, which can take up to 15 minutes. `Invoke` therefore gets `socketTimeout: 960000`, which covers that maximum plus cold start init, so a long `s3 sync` is never dropped and started again while it is still running.

**The diagram**

```mermaid
flowchart LR

classDef box fill:#eef1ff,stroke:#4c5bd4,color:#111827
classDef bad fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#cc0000,color:#111827,stroke-width:3px
classDef good fill:#c8f0c8,stroke:#008800,color:#111827,stroke-width:3px

subgraph BEFORE["BEFORE: waits until the job is killed, 1 connection"]
direction TB
  B1["cdk deploy calls DescribeStacks"] --> B2["NodeHttpHandler sends the request"]
  B2 --> B3["connection goes silent"]
  B3 --> B4{"requestTimeout 300000 passes"}
  B4 -->|"throwOnRequestTimeout not set"| B5["logs WARN and keeps waiting forever"]
  B4 -->|"response arrives"| B6["deploy continues"]
end

subgraph AFTER["AFTER: retried every 300 s, then fails with TimeoutError"]
direction TB
  A1["cdk deploy calls DescribeStacks"] --> A2["NodeHttpHandler sends the request"]
  A2 --> A3["connection goes silent"]
  A3 --> A4{"THE CHANGE: socketTimeout 300000"}
  A4 -->|"no data for 300 s"| A5["TimeoutError, retried on a new connection"]
  A4 -->|"data still moving"| A6["slow upload keeps going"]
end

B1 ~~~ A1

class B1,B2,B3,B6 box
class A1,A2,A3,A6 box
class B4,B5 bad
class A4,A5 good

linkStyle 3 stroke:#cc0000,stroke-width:5px
linkStyle 8 stroke:#008800,stroke-width:5px

style BEFORE fill:#fff5f5,stroke:#cc0000,color:#111827
style AFTER fill:#f3fff3,stroke:#008800,color:#111827
```

**The change**

- `sdkRequestHandler` now returns `socketTimeout: 300000` next to the existing `connectionTimeout` and `requestTimeout`. This is the fix. I reused the 300 seconds that `requestTimeout` already has, because the Smithy docs for `throwOnRequestTimeout` say `requestTimeout` "was for a long time incorrectly being set as a socket idle timeout". So the CLI already ran with a 5 minute idle timeout that threw for years, and this brings that behavior back on purpose.
- `SDK.lambda()` in `sdk.ts` sends `Invoke` through a second client, created on the first invoke, with `socketTimeout: 960000` and every other setting unchanged. If the caller already set `socketTimeout` to 0 (no timeout) or to something longer, `Invoke` keeps that value. The other Lambda calls, such as `UpdateFunctionCode` and the hotswap waiters, keep the shared 300 s value, so a silent one of those is not held for 16 minutes per attempt. The hotswap of a `BucketDeployment` calls `Invoke` synchronously and the function may run for the full 15 minutes, so a shorter idle timeout would drop it and the retries would start overlapping `s3 sync --delete` runs.
- `RequestHandlerSettings` in `base-credentials.ts` gets an optional `socketTimeout` field, so the value type checks and a custom `IBaseCredentialsProvider` receives it in `clientConfig.requestHandler` too.
- `requestTimeout` and its warning are left as they are. I did not turn on `throwOnRequestTimeout`, because that timer runs from the start of the request until the response headers arrive, so it would fail a healthy upload that takes longer than 5 minutes. @JimNero009 pointed this out in the issue, and their suggestion of a `socketTimeout` is what this PR follows. Thank you for the very clear report and reproduction.
- Tests in `awscli-compatible.test.ts`: one checks the settings `sdkRequestHandler` returns, including the agent on both `httpAgent` and `httpsAgent`, and fails without this change. Two more run a real `STSClient` against a local TCP server with a 1 s `socketTimeout`. To be honest about what these two prove: they pass on `main` too, because they check how Smithy handles `socketTimeout` rather than this change. I kept them as a guard in case a future Smithy version changes that behavior, but I am very happy to drop them if you would rather not have a TCP server in a unit suite: a server that never answers gets a second connection and the call rejects with `TimeoutError`; a server that sends its whole response, headers included, in small pieces every 50 ms still succeeds on one connection. That second test fails if the settings use `requestTimeout` with `throwOnRequestTimeout` instead, which is why I went with `socketTimeout`.
- Tests in `sdk.test.ts`: one checks that `invokeCommand` is sent through a client with `socketTimeout: 960000` and the other settings unchanged, and fails without this change; four check that a disabled or longer caller value is kept and a shorter or unset one is raised to 960000; one checks the `Invoke` client is created only on the first invoke; two check that other Lambda calls and the CloudFormation client still get the shared settings.

I would really value your view on a few choices, and I am happy to change any of them:

- 300 seconds restores the old behavior. Would you prefer something shorter, such as the 60 to 120 seconds the issue suggested? If so, I would be glad to check the other clients for calls that can stay silent that long, the way the Lambda one does.
- The issue also asks for these timeouts to be configurable. I left that out to keep this small, but I can add it here or in a follow up if you think it belongs.
- The standalone `cdk-assets` CLI builds its clients in `cdk-assets-lib/lib/aws.ts` without any of these timeouts. Would you like the same change there as a separate PR?

**What changes for a user**

- A deploy, bootstrap or any other command whose AWS call goes silent no longer hangs. Each silent attempt is dropped after 5 minutes and retried.
- If AWS never answers at all, the command now fails with a `TimeoutError` after the existing retries, about 35 minutes, instead of running until the CI job is killed.
- Calls that answer normally, and slow calls that keep moving data such as large asset uploads, behave exactly as before.
- `cdk deploy --hotswap` and `cdk watch` with a `BucketDeployment` that takes many minutes keep working, because `Invoke` waits up to 16 minutes.
- A call that changes state, such as `ExecuteChangeSet` or `Invoke`, is now retried after a silent timeout instead of hanging. If AWS did process the first attempt, the retry can fail with a clearer error such as an existing change set. This is the same tradeoff the SDK already makes for a reset connection.
- Proxy users are covered, because the proxy agent goes through the same `sdkRequestHandler`.
- The `requestTimeout` warning after 5 minutes still appears for very long uploads, as it does today.

Fixes #2097

### Checklist

- [ ] This change contains a major version upgrade for a dependency and I confirm all breaking changes are addressed
  - Release notes for the new version:

Fixes #2182

Running the skip STM ingest sample stopped at step 3 with a validation error, and now that step ingests the JSON events with their metadata.

**What this code is for**

`07-skip-STM/direct-ingest-api.py` shows how to send content straight to long term memory with `IngestData`, skipping short term events. Step 3 sends two JSON app events and tags the resulting records with `metadata`. The folder `README.md` shows the same call as a snippet.

**Before this PR**

A developer runs `python direct-ingest-api.py` with current boto3.

1. Steps 1 and 2 create the memory and ingest a conversation.
2. Step 3 calls `ingest(...)` with `metadata={"channel": "web", "source_system": "crm"}`.
3. `ingest` passes that through to `data.ingest_data(**request)`.
4. boto3 checks the request against the `IngestData` model, where each `metadata` value is a `MetadataValue` object.
5. It raises `ParamValidationError: Invalid type for parameter metadata.channel, value: web, type: <class 'str'>, valid types: <class 'dict'>`, and the script stops.

**After this PR**

Same developer, same command.

1. Same as above through step 1.
2. Step 3 calls `ingest(...)` with `metadata={"channel": {"stringValue": "web"}, "source_system": {"stringValue": "crm"}}`.
3. boto3 accepts the request, the JSON events are ingested, and the script continues to step 4.

issue.body:
### Issue # (if applicable)

Closes #36940.

### Reason for this change

A pipeline step that pulls in extra source folders on a Windows build image failed every run with a PowerShell syntax error; it now links those folders correctly on Windows too.

Thank you @TrevinAvery for the very clear report and repro, @SuchithraChandrasekaran for writing out the PowerShell version of the commands, and @pahud for pointing at the `!LINUX!` / `!WINDOWS!` tags and `filterBuildSpecCommands()`. This PR follows that suggestion as closely as I could. I would be grateful for any thoughts on the open questions at the end.

**What this code is for**

`CodeBuildFactory` in `pipelines/lib/codepipeline/private/codebuild-factory.ts` turns a `CodeBuildStep` or `ShellStep` into a CodeBuild project. When the step has `additionalInputs`, `generateInputArtifactLinkCommands()` writes one install command per input that links `$CODEBUILD_SRC_DIR_<artifact>` to the folder the user asked for. Later, `filterBuildSpecCommands()` drops any line tagged for the other OS, based on whether the build image is a `codebuild.WindowsBuildImage`.

**Before this PR**

A team builds on `WindowsBuildImage.WIN_SERVER_CORE_2019_BASE` with `additionalInputs: { 'package-2': input2 }`.

1. `generateInputArtifactLinkCommands()` writes one line: `[ ! -d "package-2" ] || { echo '...'; exit 1; } && ln -s -- "$CODEBUILD_SRC_DIR_..." "package-2"`.
2. The line has no `!LINUX!` or `!WINDOWS!` tag, so `filterBuildSpecCommands()` keeps it for Windows too.
3. `cdk synth` and `cdk deploy` both pass.
4. CodeBuild runs the install phase in PowerShell, which cannot read `[ ! -d ... ]`, `||` or `ln`.
5. The step stops with `Missing type name after '['` and exit code 1. I reproduced this by running the generated line in PowerShell 7.4.

### Description of changes

**After this PR**

Same team, same step.

1. `generateInputArtifactLinkCommands()` now writes two lines per input: the old bash line tagged `!LINUX!`, and a PowerShell line tagged `!WINDOWS!`.
2. `filterBuildSpecCommands()` sees a `WindowsBuildImage` and keeps only the `!WINDOWS!` line.
3. The PowerShell line runs `Test-Path -LiteralPath 'package-2'`. If the folder is already there it throws the same `additionalInputs: "package-2" must not exist yet...` message and exits 1.
4. Otherwise it runs `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force` for the parent folder (only when there is one) and `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path 'package-2' -Target $env:CODEBUILD_SRC_DIR_...`.
5. Any failure inside lands in `catch { Write-Output $_; exit 1 }`, so the step fails loudly instead of carrying on. On success the build phase starts with `package-2` in place.
6. On a Linux image, step 2 keeps the `!LINUX!` line, which is exactly the line that was generated before.

**The diagram**

```mermaid
flowchart LR

classDef box fill:#eef1ff,stroke:#4c5bd4,color:#111827
classDef bad fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#cc0000,color:#111827,stroke-width:3px
classDef good fill:#c8f0c8,stroke:#008800,color:#111827,stroke-width:3px

subgraph BEFORE["BEFORE: Windows install phase exits 1"]
direction TB
  B1["CodeBuildStep with additionalInputs"] --> B2["generateInputArtifactLinkCommands()"]
  B2 --> B3["one untagged bash line per input"]
  B3 --> B4{"filterBuildSpecCommands(): tagged?"}
  B4 -->|"untagged, kept on Windows"| B5["PowerShell parse error, exit 1"]
  B4 -->|"Linux image"| B6["bash links the input"]
end

subgraph AFTER["AFTER: Windows install phase exits 0"]
direction TB
  A1["CodeBuildStep with additionalInputs"] --> A2["generateInputArtifactLinkCommands()"]
  A2 --> A3["THE CHANGE: a !LINUX! and a !WINDOWS! line per input"]
  A3 --> A4{"filterBuildSpecCommands(): tagged for this image?"}
  A4 -->|"WindowsBuildImage"| A5["New-Item SymbolicLink links the input"]
  A4 -->|"Linux image"| A6["same bash line as before"]
end

B1 ~~~ A1

class B1,B2,B4,B6 box
class A1,A2,A4,A6 box
class B3,B5 bad
class A3,A5 good

linkStyle 3 stroke:#cc0000,stroke-width:5px
linkStyle 8 stroke:#008800,stroke-width:5px

style BEFORE fill:#fff5f5,stroke:#cc0000,color:#111827
style AFTER fill:#f3fff3,stroke:#008800,color:#111827
```

**The change**

In `generateInputArtifactLinkCommands()`, `inputs.map` becomes `inputs.flatMap` and each input returns two strings:

- `!LINUX!` plus the same bash fragments joined with `&&` as before.
- `!WINDOWS!try { ... } catch { Write-Output $_; exit 1 }` holding the `Test-Path` check, the optional parent `New-Item -ItemType Directory`, and `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink`.

A small `powershellLiteral()` puts every path in single quotes and doubles any `'` inside it, so folder names with spaces, `$` or `'` are passed as written. The `try`/`catch` is there because I found that `-ErrorAction Stop` alone, run through `pwsh -Command` in my tests, prints the error but still ends with exit code 0.

No change to `filterBuildSpecCommands()` or to how the OS is picked. The tags are the same ones `dockerCredentialsInstallCommands()` already uses.

**What changes for a user**

- Steps with `additionalInputs` on a Windows build image now link their inputs instead of failing in the install phase.
- An input folder that already exists still stops the build with the same message on both OSes.
- Nested folders such as `some/deep/directory` and parent paths such as `../sibling` work on both OSes.
- Linux builds get the same buildspec text as today, so existing projects see no diff.
- Windows projects that use `additionalInputs` will see their buildspec change on the next deploy, which restarts that pipeline once.

### Describe any new or updated permissions being added

None.

### Description of how you validated changes

- Unit tests in `pipelines/test/codepipeline/codebuild-step.test.ts` for a Windows image with two inputs (one nested, one `../sibling`) and for a folder name containing a space, `$` and `'`. Both fail on `main` and pass with this change. The existing Linux tests, including the exact strings in `synths.test.ts`, pass unchanged. All 22 `pipelines` test suites pass, along with `eslint` and `tsc`.
- I took the synthesized `!WINDOWS!` lines and ran them in PowerShell 7.4 (macOS): first run links all three inputs and exits 0, second run hits the "must not exist yet" message and exits 1, and a blocked path exits 1.
- I do not have a Windows CodeBuild project to run this on, so there is no integration test run here. I would be very thankful if a maintainer could run one, or let me know if you would like me to add an integ test for a maintainer to deploy.
- If it seems fair to you, could this PR get the `pr-linter/exempt-integ-test` label? There is no Windows CodeBuild integ setup to snapshot against yet, and the unit tests check the generated lines exactly. I am very happy to add an integ test instead if you prefer.

A few questions where your view would really help:

1. `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink` mirrors `ln -s` and worked in my runs, and as far as I know CodeBuild Windows runs as an administrator. Would you prefer `-ItemType Junction`, which needs no special rights but only works for folders on the same drive?
2. @TrevinAvery mentioned that some people switch the Windows shell to `cmd`. This PR targets PowerShell, the default. Would you like `cmd` handled here, or left for a follow up?

### Checklist

- [x] My code adheres to the [CONTRIBUTING GUIDE](https://github.com/aws/aws-cdk/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [DESIGN GUIDELINES](https://github.com/aws/aws-cdk/blob/main/docs/DESIGN_GUIDELINES.md)

---

issue.title: [FEATURE] Public in-process test harness for BedrockAgentCoreApp
issue.body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

Unit-testing an agent built on `BedrockAgentCoreApp` today means binding a real port, sending HTTP, and parsing SSE text by hand. The SDK's own tests sidestep this by reaching into the private Fastify instance (`app['_app'].inject(...)`, ~40 call sites in `src/runtime/__tests__`). That's a good signal the in-process path is the useful one for tests, but users can't reach it without depending on a private field.

#300 / #301 (`listen()` / `close()`) make the real-server path cleaner. This proposal is the complementary no-network path.

### Describe the solution you'd like

A small public, test-oriented API that:

- invokes the invocation handler in-process (no port),
- lets you set what AgentCore Runtime would send (session ID, request ID, custom headers),
- returns the streamed events as parsed objects instead of raw SSE text,
- surfaces `requestSchema` validation failures as a normal result so tests can assert on them.

Shipped from a `/testing` subpath so it never lands in production bundles.

### Proposed API

```ts
import { createTestClient } from 'bedrock-agentcore/runtime/testing'

const client = createTestClient(app)

const result = await client.invoke({ prompt: 'hi' }, { sessionId: 'test-session' })
expect(result.status).toBe(200)
expect(result.events).toEqual([{ event: 'message', data: { text: 'you said hi' } }])

const bad = await client.invoke({ wrong: true })
expect(bad.status).toBe(400)

const ping = await client.ping()
expect(ping.status).toBe('Healthy')
```

Names are illustrative. WebSocket handlers are out of scope for a first version.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

- `listen()` on an ephemeral port + `fetch` + an SSE parser (what #301 enables): works, but slower, needs teardown, and every user rewrites SSE parsing.
- Calling `app['_app'].inject` directly: depends on a private field.
- On the Python side, `BedrockAgentCoreApp` is a Starlette app, so users get Starlette's `TestClient` for free. The TS app wraps Fastify, so there's no equivalent today.

### Use Case

Fast unit tests and CI for agent handlers, regression tests on the exact event sequence a handler streams, and a foundation for assertion-style agent evals.

### Additional context

Inspiration: agent frameworks such as the Botpress ADK make "invoke this piece of the agent once and assert on what it did" a first-class part of the dev loop. A tiny public harness gives TS AgentCore users the same fast loop.

Would love maintainer input on whether this belongs in the SDK and on the API shape. cc @jariy17 @aidandaly24, and @ioanlucut since it sits next to #300.

### Would you be willing to contribute this feature?

- [ ] Yes
- [ ] No

Do any of them fit where you'd like the TypeScript SDK to go? If one does, I'd be glad to put up a PR for it, or to reshape the proposal however works best for you.

issue.title: fix(auth): respect OAuthError thrown by verifyToken
issue.body:
When a token check rejects a request on purpose, the server now sends the answer that check chose and no longer prints the error to the logs.

**What this code is for**

`withMcpAuth` in `src/auth/auth-wrapper.ts` sits in front of an MCP route. On every request it reads the bearer token, passes it to the `verifyToken` function the app provides, and then either calls the route handler or answers with a challenge built by `bearerAuthChallengeResponse` (401 for `invalid_token`, 403 for `insufficient_scope`, 500 for `server_error`). Since #63, a verifier can throw `OAuthError` to say exactly why a token was refused.

**Before this PR**

A client calls the MCP route with a token that is valid but lacks a scope, and the app's verifier knows it.

1. `withMcpAuth` calls `verifyToken(req, bearerToken)`.
2. The verifier throws `new OAuthError(OAuthErrorCode.InsufficientScope, "Rejected by verifier")`.
3. The first `catch` runs `console.error("Unexpected error authenticating bearer token:", error)`, so the whole error object and stack go to the platform logs.
4. It then throws the verifier's error away and builds `new OAuthError(OAuthErrorCode.InvalidToken, "Invalid token")`.
5. The client gets 401 `invalid_token` instead of 403 `insufficient_scope`, and a verifier that throws `server_error` for a database outage also gets 401.

**After this PR**

Same client, same token, same verifier.

1. Same as above through step 2.
2. The first `catch` checks `OAuthError.isInstance(error)` before anything else.
3. It is an `OAuthError`, so it goes straight to `bearerAuthChallengeResponse(error, challengeOptions)` with no log line.
4. The client gets 403 `insufficient_scope` with the `WWW-Authenticate` header listing the required scopes.
5. If the verifier throws a plain `Error` instead, nothing changes: it is logged as today and the client gets 401 `invalid_token`.

**The diagram**

```mermaid
flowchart LR

classDef box fill:#eef1ff,stroke:#4c5bd4,color:#111827
classDef bad fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#cc0000,color:#111827,stroke-width:3px
classDef good fill:#c8f0c8,stroke:#008800,color:#111827,stroke-width:3px

subgraph BEFORE["BEFORE: 401 and a full log line"]
direction TB
  B1["client calls the MCP route"] --> B2["verifyToken throws"]
  B2 --> B3["first catch in withMcpAuth"]
  B3 --> B4{"no type check"}
  B4 -->|"OAuthError insufficient_scope"| B5["console.error full error, 401 invalid_token"]
  B4 -->|"plain Error"| B6["console.error full error, 401 invalid_token"]
end

subgraph AFTER["AFTER: 403 and no log line"]
direction TB
  A1["client calls the MCP route"] --> A2["verifyToken throws"]
  A2 --> A3["first catch in withMcpAuth"]
  A3 --> A4{"THE CHANGE: OAuthError.isInstance(error)"}
  A4 -->|"OAuthError insufficient_scope"| A5["no log, 403 insufficient_scope"]
  A4 -->|"plain Error"| A6["console.error, 401 invalid_token, as today"]
end

B1 ~~~ A1

class B1,B2,B3,B6 box
class A1,A2,A3,A6 box
class B4,B5 bad
class A4,A5 good

linkStyle 3 stroke:#cc0000,stroke-width:5px
linkStyle 8 stroke:#008800,stroke-width:5px

style BEFORE fill:#fff5f5,stroke:#cc0000,color:#111827
style AFTER fill:#f3fff3,stroke:#008800,color:#111827
```

**The change**

Three lines at the top of the `catch` around `verifyToken`:

```ts
if (OAuthError.isInstance(error)) {
  return bearerAuthChallengeResponse(error, challengeOptions);
}
```

This is the first fix @Ramp-co suggested in #198, and it copies what the second `catch` in the same function already does for the expiry and scope checks. The decision uses the error's type, not its message. Untyped errors keep the existing `console.error` and 401 on purpose, so nobody's behavior changes unless their verifier already throws `OAuthError`.

Tests in `tests/auth-wrapper.test.ts` cover a verifier throwing `invalid_token` (401), `insufficient_scope` (403) and `server_error` (500), each with no `console.error` call, plus a plain `Error` that is still logged and still answered with 401. The three typed cases fail on `main`. A patch changeset is included.

**What changes for a user**

- A verifier that throws `OAuthError` now controls the status, code and description the client receives, and its error is no longer logged by the library.
- The message of a thrown `OAuthError` is now sent to the client as `error_description`, so verifiers should keep it free of internal details.
- A verifier can report an outage as 500 by throwing `OAuthError(OAuthErrorCode.ServerError, ...)`, which covers the 5xx case raised in the issue without changing the default.
- Verifiers that return `undefined`, return `AuthInfo`, or throw a plain `Error` behave exactly as before.
- I left out the second idea from the issue, the redacted default log with a `logAuthErrors` option that would also cover the `MCP handler error:` log in `src/handler/mcp-api-handler.ts`, because it adds public API and felt like your call. Would you like that here, in a follow up PR, or not at all?
- I also kept plain `Error` throws at 401 rather than 500, since moving them would change today's responses. Would you prefer them to go through `bearerAuthChallengeResponse` and become 500 like the second `catch` does? Happy to go whichever way you think is best.

Refs #198

Just checking in on this one: when `verifyToken` throws an `OAuthError`, the handler now answers with the status that error chose instead of logging it. Is there anything I could change or explain that would make it easier to review?

issue.title: fix(functions): run the SDK bin entry when no .bin shim exists
issue.body:
### Description

Deploying functions on Windows with Bun stopped because the CLI could not find the Functions SDK, and now it runs the SDK's own declared entry file instead.

**What this code is for**

`findFunctionsBinary()` in `src/deploy/functions/runtimes/node/index.ts` finds the program inside the `firebase-functions` package that reads a codebase and reports its functions. `spawnFunctionsProcess()` runs that program during `firebase deploy` and in the emulator, and the CLI builds the deploy plan from what it reports.

**Before this PR**

A developer on Windows installs dependencies with `bun install` and runs `firebase deploy --only functions`, as @philemonkipngetich described in #11386.

1. `spawnFunctionsProcess()` calls `findFunctionsBinary()`.

issue.title: Colour functions and contract components by how recently their code changed
issue.body:
It is hard to see which parts of a project changed lately. The Functions list and the Contract diagram show every item the same way, so the newest work does not stand out from code nobody has touched in months.

**Ask**

- Functions tab: each row gets a recency colour from the git history of that function's own lines. Uncommitted edits count as the newest.
- Contract tab: each component gets the colour of the newest change across the files and functions it covers. External components with no code stay neutral.
- The scale is ranked against this repo's own dates, so a repo touched only last year still shows a spread and one outlier does not flatten it.
- A small legend (newest to oldest) and a tooltip with the relative date and the commit subject.
- A "Recent" sort next to Importance, Lines and Name.

**Edge cases**

Not a git repo, shallow clone, untracked files, a repo with no commits, large repos (batched, cached by HEAD and dirty files, never blocking the UI), and projects opened from a worktree.

issue.title: Contract draft draws top level folders instead of an architecture flow chart
issue.body:
## Problem

"Draft with Claude" on the Contract tab draws the repo's top level folders, not its architecture. For the HEAG bot (Reggie AI, a Botpress ADK bot that answers Title IV compliance questions) it drew four boxes: `scripts`, `skills`, `tests`, each with an arrow into `src`. That is the same thing the Code tab already shows without AI, so the contract tells you nothing.

The cause is in `electron/draft/draft.ts`: `evidence()` groups files by their top level folder and hands those folders to Claude as the components, the prompt says "Use exactly these component ids and no others", and `validate()` drops any component that is not one of those folders. Claude has no way to answer with anything else.

Many existing `architect.md` files drafted this way are now sitting in repos with the same folder boxes.

## Intended behavior

The contract is an architecture flow chart:

- Nodes are runtime components. For a bot that means things like the conversation handler, the model call, each tool, knowledge base retrieval, the refresh workflow, tables and outside services.
- Edges point the way a request or data moves, and each edge is labelled with what moves along it.
- It is built on the function index Architect already has. The Functions tab lists every function with its file, summary, "used in N places" count, importance and the call graph, all without AI. That index and call graph go to Claude as the main input in place of the folder list. Claude groups the functions into components by what they do and labels the flows; the call graph between the groups is used to draw edges Claude leaves out.
- Each node points at the real functions and files it covers, so the drawing is grounded in the code.
- A reply whose components are just the top level folders is rejected and asked for again with the reason. If it comes back as folders twice, the draft fails with a clear message instead of showing a folder tree.
- An existing contract that only lists top level folders is flagged on the Contract tab with a one click "Redraw as a flow chart".
- The canvas shows edge labels and leaves room for them in the layout.

issue.title: Custom command {{args}} and system prompt substitution expand `$` replacement patterns

labels.name: user-6ec56081/repo-566d0f35
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: user-3ef72433/repo-efde29d2
labels.description: Issues related to User Interface, OS Support, Core Functionality

labels.name: user-3784fdbb/repo-a70605d4
labels.description: 1 day or less: trivial logic, UI adjustments, docs

issue.body:
### What happened?

When a custom command's `{{args}}` (or a system prompt placeholder) is filled in, any `$` patterns in the inserted text get expanded by JavaScript instead of being kept as typed.

Custom commands insert whatever the user typed after the command into the prompt at `{{args}}`. The docs promise this text is "injected exactly as the user typed them" ([custom-commands.md#L71](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/6814e00d6b148c3a1d57244d5d7040f7c541009d/docs/cli/custom-commands.md?plain=1#L71)).

The substitution passes the user's text as the replacement _string_ to `replaceAll` ([shellProcessor.ts#L73](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/6814e00d6b148c3a1d57244d5d7040f7c541009d/packages/cli/src/services/prompt-processors/shellProcessor.ts#L73), [#L93](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/6814e00d6b148c3a1d57244d5d7040f7c541009d/packages/cli/src/services/prompt-processors/shellProcessor.ts#L93), [#L158](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/6814e00d6b148c3a1d57244d5d7040f7c541009d/packages/cli/src/services/prompt-processors/shellProcessor.ts#L158), [#L210](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/6814e00d6b148c3a1d57244d5d7040f7c541009d/packages/cli/src/services/prompt-processors/shellProcessor.ts#L210)), so JS treats `$$`, `$&`, `` $` `` and `$'` in it as special patterns.

1. Have a custom command whose prompt is something like `say {{args}}`.
2. Run `/explain costs $$5 and $&`.
3. The model receives `say costs $5 and {{args}}`: `$$` collapsed to `$`, and `$&` turned back into the literal placeholder.

`applySubstitutions` in `packages/core/src/prompts/utils.ts` has the same pattern for `${AgentSkills}`, `${SubAgents}` and `${AvailableTools}` ([#L72](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/6814e00d6b148c3a1d57244d5d7040f7c541009d/packages/core/src/prompts/utils.ts#L72), [#L85](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/6814e00d6b148c3a1d57244d5d7040f7c541009d/packages/core/src/prompts/utils.ts#L85), [#L93](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/6814e00d6b148c3a1d57244d5d7040f7c541009d/packages/core/src/prompts/utils.ts#L93)), so a skill or subagent description containing a `$` pattern would also be altered in the system prompt.

### What did you expect to happen?

The text should arrive exactly as typed: `say costs $$5 and $&`.

Minimal repro in plain Node:

```js
"say {{args}}".replaceAll("{{args}}", "costs $$5 and $&");
// => 'say costs $5 and {{args}}'

"say {{args}}".replaceAll("{{args}}", () => "costs $$5 and $&");
// => 'say costs $$5 and $&'
```

### Client information

Found by reading the source on main at 6814e00 (source review, not a running client).

### Login information

N/A

### Anything else we need to know?

This looks like the same class as #29044, which #30035 fixed really nicely for the summarizer, llm edit fixer and session summary. Thanks for that work! These two spots just weren't in its scope. The `applySubstitutions` half was also raised in #27993, which went stale and was closed.

Which fix would you prefer here: a replacer function (`() => value`) or `split().join()`? Happy to send a small PR with tests if you're open to adding `help wanted`.

issue.body:
Fixes #333

The NVIDIA driver page now tells people to upgrade below driver 575, matching the minimum the same page states, instead of below 525.

**What this code is for**

`docs/how-to/setup/drivers.md` is the setup page people follow before installing an inference snap on a machine with an NVIDIA GPU. It says which driver version is needed, how to check the installed one, and how to install a newer one.

**Before this PR**

A person with `nvidia-driver-550` installed follows the NVIDIA GPU section.

1. The page says inference snaps use CUDA Toolkit 12.9 and need driver **575 or higher**.
2. They run `apt list --installed nvidia-driver*` and see 550.
3. The next line says to upgrade only "if the installed version is lower than 525".
4. 550 is not lower than 525, so they skip the upgrade.
5. They keep a driver that is too old for CUDA Toolkit 12.9.

**After this PR**

Same person, same section.

1. Same as above through step 2.
2. The next line says to upgrade "if the installed version is lower than 575".
3. 550 is lower than 575, so they run `sudo apt install nvidia-driver-xxx`.
4. The example under it now reads `575`, so the version they pick meets the minimum.

A node's `errorHandler` runs again on resume when a parallel sibling interrupted, although it already finished

comment.body:
Thanks @yifanxiong272 for such a clean repro, the `handled` counter made it really easy to see. I traced it to the same spot in `_resumeErrorHandlersIfApplicable`: on resume the handler task gets scheduled again, but nothing hands its saved writes back, so the runner sees empty writes and calls it a second time.

I'm putting up a small fix that passes the handler task through `_reapplyWritesToSucceededNodes` right after it's scheduled. A handler that finished keeps its writes and is skipped, while a handler that interrupted or never ran still runs. Python has the same gap (langchain-ai/langgraph#9002), and the attempt there (langchain-ai/langgraph#9034) went the same way, so the two should line up.

@harshitsharmaaaa I saw you offered to take this too, sorry if I'm stepping on it. If you already have something going, I'm happy to close mine.

One question for the maintainers: would you rather this live in `_resumeErrorHandlersIfApplicable` like I have it, or should the runner skip a handler whose writes are already saved? Happy to move it either way.

issue.title: feat(review): review each commit of a PR separately
issue.body:
With per commit review turned on by the host, `/review` reviews each commit of a PR on its own diff and commit message, instead of only the combined diff.

Closes #4470. It is opt in and host only. The commit messages piece was split out into #4603, as suggested, and that has now landed on `main`.

**What this code is for**

`PRReviewer.run()` in `pr_agent/commands/pr_reviewer.py` handles `/review`. It asks the git provider for the PR diff, renders `pr_reviewer_prompts.toml` with that diff, makes one model call (or a few when chunking), and publishes one review comment.

**Before this PR**

A maintainer on GitLab has an MR with 4 commits, each with a message that explains one change, and comments `/review`.

1. `PRReviewer.run()` asks `GitLabProvider.get_diff_files()` for the diff of the whole MR.
2. The prompt gets that combined diff, plus the title and description.
3. The model returns findings with file and line, but nothing says which commit a finding belongs to.
4. One review comment for the whole MR. The maintainer has to work out by hand which of the 4 commits needs the fixup.

**After this PR**

Same maintainer, same MR, with `per_commit_review = true` in the host config or `.pr_agent.toml`.

1. `PRReviewer.run()` sees `per_commit_review` and calls `_run_per_commit()`.
2. `get_pr_commits()` returns the 4 commits, oldest first, with their parents, read fresh from the provider on every run. Merge commits are dropped here without loading them. `_commit_review_records()` reads the commits already reviewed from hidden markers in PR-Agent's own comments. For each commit not already listed by SHA, `set_commit_review_scope()` loads its files once and returns a fingerprint of its own patch, and only commits whose fingerprint is not recorded are kept. On the first run there are no markers, so all 4 are kept.
3. For each commit, `set_commit_review_scope()` scopes the diff to that commit against its parent, and `commit_under_review` puts its message (clipped to `max_commits_tokens`) in the prompt, between random markers made fresh for each run. `commit_messages_str` is cleared, so the prompt does not also list every other commit's message.
4. `_run_review()` runs once per commit and publishes one comment that names and links the commit. It uses the incremental review header, so it never replaces the persistent full review.
5. A commit with no findings gets no comment when `pr_reviewer.publish_output_no_suggestions = false`. With `inline_key_issues = true`, findings land inline on that commit's own diff.
6. 4 comments, one per commit, each with a `<!-- pr-agent:reviewed-commit <fingerprint> <sha> -->` line two lines below the hidden `<!-- pr-agent:review:incremental -->` identity. On the next push with 1 new commit, only that commit is reviewed. Without the setting, `/review` takes exactly the old path.

**The diagram**

```mermaid
flowchart LR

classDef box fill:#eef1ff,stroke:#4c5bd4,color:#111827
classDef bad fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#cc0000,color:#111827,stroke-width:3px
classDef good fill:#c8f0c8,stroke:#008800,color:#111827,stroke-width:3px

subgraph BEFORE["BEFORE: 1 review for 4 commits"]
direction TB
  B1["Maintainer comments /review"] --> B2["PRReviewer.run"]
  B2 --> B3["get_diff_files for the whole MR"]
  B3 --> B4{"one prompt, combined diff"}
  B4 -->|"findings not tied to a commit"| B5["1 comment for the whole MR"]
  B4 -->|"per_commit_review off"| B6["same as today"]
end

subgraph AFTER["AFTER: 1 review per commit"]
direction TB
  A1["Maintainer comments /review"] --> A2["PRReviewer.run"]
  A2 --> A3["get_pr_commits"]
  A3 --> A4{"THE CHANGE: per_commit_review on"}
  A4 -->|"each commit: own diff and message"| A5["1 comment per commit, linked"]
  A4 -->|"setting off or provider unsupported"| A6["whole PR review, as today"]
end

B1 ~~~ A1

class B1,B2,B3,B6 box
class A1,A2,A3,A6 box
class B4,B5 bad
class A4,A5 good

linkStyle 3 stroke:#cc0000,stroke-width:5px
linkStyle 8 stroke:#008800,stroke-width:5px

style BEFORE fill:#fff5f5,stroke:#cc0000,color:#111827
style AFTER fill:#f3fff3,stroke:#008800,color:#111827
```

**The change**

* `PRReviewer.run()` now branches on `per_commit_review` into `_run_per_commit()`, and the old body moved into `_run_review()` unchanged apart from the commit header and the checks below.
* `GitProvider` gets `get_pr_commits()` (returns `None` by default, so other providers fall back to a whole PR review with a notice) and `set_commit_review_scope()`. GitHub and GitLab implement both on top of the existing incremental diff path. On GitHub, new side file contents are read at the commit when a head SHA is set.
* `_run_per_commit()` reviews only commits whose fingerprint is not recorded, so a plain `/review` and the default `push_commands` no longer review every commit again on each push (454174f1, 40cb6ee2, b52fbf25, bf4dd1b6, 9b159195). `commit_patch_fingerprint()` in `git_provider.py` hashes each file's name and patch with the `@@ -a,b +c,d @@` numbers removed, so a rebase onto `main` that leaves a commit's own patch alone does not review it again, while an amend or `--autosquash` fixup does. On GitLab, when a file's diff comes back empty (collapsed, too large or binary), the commit SHA is mixed into the fingerprint so two different commits never share one; such a commit is reviewed again after a rebase. A commit is recorded only after its review succeeds, including when every file was filtered out: `_run_review()` puts the marker line two lines below the comment's hidden incremental review identity, and a commit that gets no comment (no findings with `publish_output_no_suggestions = false`) goes into one record comment that starts with `<!-- pr-agent:review:commits -->` and is edited in place through `publish_persistent_comment_full()`. With default settings and no merge commits, no record comment is created. Before writing, the record is read again and merged, trimmed to commits still in the PR, and cut from the oldest end if it would pass the 65000 character comment limit. Markers count only at those fixed lines and only in comments `is_comment_authored_by_pr_agent()` confirms. A marker in a comment confirmed as someone else's is ignored. Markers are found by that hidden identity rather than the visible heading, so changing `review_heading` never reviews commits again. When comment authorship cannot be checked for the run, or marker comments exist but none can be confirmed and the author of at least one cannot be verified (for example a GitHub App whose login cannot be resolved), the run falls back to one whole PR review with a notice instead of reviewing every commit on each push. Each commit's files are loaded once per run and reused for its review; a commit whose patch is already recorded under another SHA (a rebase) is recorded under the new SHA too, and a commit with no changes of its own is recorded, so neither is loaded again. A failed commit is not recorded, so the next run retries it; the record counts failed attempts, and automatic runs stop after `PER_COMMIT_MAX_AUTO_ATTEMPTS` (3) while a manual `/review` always retries. Selection does not use commit dates, so a commit authored before the last review but pushed after it is still reviewed. If the comments cannot be read, the run fails with the usual failure comment instead of reviewing every commit. The `-i` lookup and its `minimal_*_for_incremental_review` thresholds are not used here, so a manual `/review` never stops silently. `docs/docs/commands/review.md` says so, and also says that if PR-Agent's comments are removed, the next run reviews every commit again unless `max_commits_per_review` is set (93cb7440).
* The commit message block opens and closes with `{{ commit_message_begin }}` and `{{ commit_message_end }}` from `prompt_boundary_markers("COMMIT_MESSAGE")` (the helper #4603 added to `pr_agent/algo/artifacts.py`), so a commit message containing `<<<COMMIT_MESSAGE_END>>>` cannot close the block early. It sits right above #4603's `commit_messages_str` block, which keeps its own `COMMIT_MESSAGES` markers.
* `_should_publish_review_no_suggestions()` checks the parsed findings for a commit review, so a commit where the model returned nothing or prose stays quiet with `publish_output_no_suggestions = false`.
* `per_commit_review` and `max_commits_per_review` are in the `pr_reviewer` entry of `CLI_HOST_ONLY_KEYS_BY_SECTION` and `PER_DIRECTORY_HOST_ONLY_KEYS_BY_SECTION`, so `/review --pr_reviewer.per_commit_review=true` in a comment is rejected.
* `max_commits_per_review` defaults to 0 (no limit). When more commits than the cap are not reviewed yet, the whole PR is reviewed once with a notice, and after that review succeeds all its commits are recorded, so the next push goes back to one review per new commit. GitHub lists at most 250 commits per PR, so a PR with more is reviewed as a whole with a notice.
* Merge commits, root commits and empty commits are skipped. One failing commit does not stop the rest; the run is marked failed afterwards.
* Upstream `main` is merged in with merge commits (181edc4c, 9723af3a), not a rebase, so no history is rewritten. Conflicts: `convert_to_markdown_v2()` keeps main's `get_bot_display_name()` next to the commit header, `CLI_HOST_ONLY_KEYS_BY_SECTION` keeps main's new `pr_reviewer` keys plus ours, and the key count in `test_config_reference.py` is main's 319 plus our 2. After #4798, `run()` no longer checks `is_answer`, and the tests set `config.is_auto_command`. After #4838 renamed `pr_agent/tools` to `pr_agent/commands`, the tests import from `pr_agent.commands` and the config links point at `../commands/review.md` (ed7715a5). `_prepare_code_suggestions()` on GitHub skips `validate_comments_inside_hunks()` while a commit scope is set, so a finding outside that commit's diff stays in the commit's summary instead of moving to a nearby line. `pytest tests/unittest` on 912963d8: 17692 passed, 34 skipped. `ruff check`: clean.

**What changes for a user**

* Nothing unless the host turns on `per_commit_review`. Default `/review` is unchanged.
* With it on: one model call per reviewed commit. The first run reviews every commit, and later runs review only new commits or commits whose own changes changed, so `-i` is no longer needed in `push_commands`.
* Each commit's review sees only that commit's diff, so it can flag something a later commit fixes, or miss a helper added in an earlier commit.
* Only GitHub and GitLab support it. Other providers get the usual whole PR review with a one line notice.

comment.body:
Hi all, hope you're doing well! Now that #4603 has landed (thank you for the reviews on that one), I merged `main` back into this branch in efb5815b so it's no longer conflicting.

The overlap was small: the per commit message block now sits next to the commit messages block from #4603, each with its own markers, and I shortened the `per_commit_review` config line to fit the new 160 character limit. Unit tests and ruff are green. Still happy to leave this parked until there's data on review quality, as discussed.

issue.title: Custom command {{args}} and system prompt substitution expand `$` replacement patterns

labels.name: user-6ec56081/repo-566d0f35
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: user-3ef72433/repo-efde29d2
labels.description: Issues related to User Interface, OS Support, Core Functionality

labels.name: user-3784fdbb/repo-a70605d4
labels.description: 1 day or less: trivial logic, UI adjustments, docs

issue.body:
### What happened?

When a custom command's `{{args}}` (or a system prompt placeholder) is filled in, any `$` patterns in the inserted text get expanded by JavaScript instead of being kept as typed.

Custom commands insert whatever the user typed after the command into the prompt at `{{args}}`. The docs promise this text is "injected exactly as the user typed them" ([custom-commands.md#L71](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/6814e00d6b148c3a1d57244d5d7040f7c541009d/docs/cli/custom-commands.md?plain=1#L71)).

The substitution passes the user's text as the replacement _string_ to `replaceAll` ([shellProcessor.ts#L73](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/6814e00d6b148c3a1d57244d5d7040f7c541009d/packages/cli/src/services/prompt-processors/shellProcessor.ts#L73), [#L93](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/6814e00d6b148c3a1d57244d5d7040f7c541009d/packages/cli/src/services/prompt-processors/shellProcessor.ts#L93), [#L158](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/6814e00d6b148c3a1d57244d5d7040f7c541009d/packages/cli/src/services/prompt-processors/shellProcessor.ts#L158), [#L210](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/6814e00d6b148c3a1d57244d5d7040f7c541009d/packages/cli/src/services/prompt-processors/shellProcessor.ts#L210)), so JS treats `$$`, `$&`, `` $` `` and `$'` in it as special patterns.

1. Have a custom command whose prompt is something like `say {{args}}`.
2. Run `/explain costs $$5 and $&`.
3. The model receives `say costs $5 and {{args}}`: `$$` collapsed to `$`, and `$&` turned back into the literal placeholder.

`applySubstitutions` in `packages/core/src/prompts/utils.ts` has the same pattern for `${AgentSkills}`, `${SubAgents}` and `${AvailableTools}` ([#L72](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/6814e00d6b148c3a1d57244d5d7040f7c541009d/packages/core/src/prompts/utils.ts#L72), [#L85](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/6814e00d6b148c3a1d57244d5d7040f7c541009d/packages/core/src/prompts/utils.ts#L85), [#L93](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/6814e00d6b148c3a1d57244d5d7040f7c541009d/packages/core/src/prompts/utils.ts#L93)), so a skill or subagent description containing a `$` pattern would also be altered in the system prompt.

### What did you expect to happen?

The text should arrive exactly as typed: `say costs $$5 and $&`.

Minimal repro in plain Node:

```js
"say {{args}}".replaceAll("{{args}}", "costs $$5 and $&");
// => 'say costs $5 and {{args}}'

"say {{args}}".replaceAll("{{args}}", () => "costs $$5 and $&");
// => 'say costs $$5 and $&'
```

### Client information

Found by reading the source on main at 6814e00 (source review, not a running client).

### Login information

N/A

### Anything else we need to know?

This looks like the same class as #29044, which #30035 fixed really nicely for the summarizer, llm edit fixer and session summary. Thanks for that work! These two spots just weren't in its scope. The `applySubstitutions` half was also raised in #27993, which went stale and was closed.

Which fix would you prefer here: a replacer function (`() => value`) or `split().join()`? Happy to send a small PR with tests if you're open to adding `help wanted`.

comment.body: Hey @ANUBprad, thanks so much for jumping in, and for reading through both files so carefully! Your plan with replacer callbacks plus tests for raw and escaped `{{args}}` sounds right to me. So everyone has the full picture: @tanveerhkit opened #30115 a little while ago with the same approach. From what I can see it covers every spot, including the escaped `{{args}}` that goes into `!{...}` shell commands. I'd offered a PR too, but I'm very happy to step back so we don't end up with three PRs for one small fix. Maintainers, would you like to go with #30115, or would you prefer @ANUBprad take it? Either works great for me.

Thank you, this was a great catch. I had trusted `$#` as the count of slots to clear, so a seeded `env '#=5000'` (or a far bigger one) turned setup into a long synchronous loop, and a non numeric `$#` even skipped setting the arguments.

In 13c0ad6 and 6ce40bb, scripts, `source` and function calls no longer read `$#` for this. They walk the numbered parameters that really exist (`$1` through `$9`, then onward while they are set), the same walk `set --` already uses, so the work is bounded by real state rather than by a hard error or a clamp. 1681b39 also clears the callee's parameters before restoring the caller's, so `set --` inside a function or a sourced file no longer leaks back. The new tests cover a seeded `$#` of 1e9 with `maxArrayElements` and `maxLoopIterations` at 10, a non numeric `$#`, and parameters set past `$#`.

One question: `shift` still loops up to `$#` in the same way, and that was there before this PR. Would you like me to fix it here, or in a separate PR?
